question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
answer:
Yes. Alec can have Eternal Witness's enters-the-battlefield trigger target the Elspeth Conquers Death card in his graveyard.

Why: Chapter III of Elspeth Conquers Death resolves, returning Eternal Witness to the battlefield, and Eternal Witness's ability ("When this creature enters, you may return target card from your graveyard to your hand") triggers. Elspeth Conquers Death is only sacrificed once its chapter ability has left the stack — that's a state-based action that doesn't use the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11] — so Elspeth Conquers Death is put into Alec's graveyard as chapter III finishes resolving, before anyone gets priority again. Targets for a triggered ability are chosen as the ability is put on the stack [115.1d], which happens after that sacrifice, so the Elspeth Conquers Death card is already a legal card in Alec's graveyard at the moment Eternal Witness's trigger is targeted.

This is the same principle as the Eternal Witness ruling that its ability can target a card put into your graveyard as the spell that returned it resolves [Eternal Witness ruling #0].

On resolution, Eternal Witness's trigger returns the Elspeth Conquers Death card to Alec's hand (the "may" is optional). Note nothing about the trigger already on the stack changes if the Saga leaves the battlefield [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #6].

Player count doesn't matter here — this works identically in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Alec's own permanents and graveyard are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.603.3: Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.” The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere.
gold_text.704.5s: The state-based actions are as follows: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”
gold_text.714.4: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number, and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

cited_text.115.1d: Some spells and abilities require their controller to choose one or more targets for them. The targets are object(s) and/or player(s) the spell or ability will affect. These targets are declared as part of the process of putting the spell or ability on the stack. The targets can’t be changed except by another spell or ability that explicitly says it can do so. A triggered ability is targeted if it identifies something it will affect by using the phrase “target [something],” where the “something” is a phrase that describes an object and/or player. The target(s) are chosen as the ability is put on the stack; see rule 603.3d.

answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
Yes — assuming an opponent has lost life this turn, Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using one {C}.

Why: Robber of the Rich says that during any turn you attacked with a Rogue, you may cast the exiled card "and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." Under rule 609.4b, an effect that lets you spend mana as though it were mana of any color affects only how you may pay a cost — it doesn't change the cost itself and doesn't change what mana was actually spent. So the cost is still {R}, but colorless mana ({C}) may be spent to pay that {R}. Note {C} is normally colorless-specific mana and is not generic and not interchangeable with colored symbols; only Robber of the Rich's "as though" effect makes this work here.

The spectacle cost is an alternative cost: rule 702.137a says "Spectacle [cost]" means you may pay that cost rather than the spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn, following the alternative-cost rules in 601.2b and 601.2f–h. Light Up the Stage's mana cost is {2}{R} and its spectacle cost is {R}, so paying spectacle means paying exactly one red-requiring symbol — satisfied here by {C} via Robber of the Rich.

Conditions Autumn still needs:
- An opponent must have lost life this turn. If Robber of the Rich's combat damage got through to Nehemiah, that counts (damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life — Light Up the Stage ruling #4). Spectacle cares only that life was lost at some point this turn, even if it was later gained back (Light Up the Stage ruling #6), and the cost is {R} regardless of how much life was lost or how many opponents lost it (ruling #7).
- Timing: Light Up the Stage is a sorcery. Neither Robber of the Rich nor spectacle changes when it can be cast (Robber of the Rich ruling #6; Light Up the Stage ruling #8), so Autumn must cast it during their own main phase with an empty stack — realistically the postcombat main phase of the turn Robber of the Rich attacked (or a later turn on which Autumn again attacks with a Rogue, per Robber of the Rich ruling #5).

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any table size. Spectacle only requires that some opponent lost life this turn — it need not be Nehemiah, the defending player whose library was raided. In a multiplayer game, if the opponent who lost life later leaves the game, Autumn can still use spectacle that turn (Light Up the Stage ruling #3).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.118.9a: Some spells have alternative costs. An alternative cost is a cost listed in a spell’s text, or applied to it from another effect, that its controller may pay rather than paying the spell’s mana cost. Alternative costs are usually phrased, “You may [action] rather than pay [this object’s] mana cost,” or “You may cast [this object] without paying its mana cost.” Note that some alternative costs are listed in keywords; see rule 702. Only one alternative cost can be applied to any one spell as it’s being cast. The controller of the spell announces their intentions to pay that cost as described in rule 601.2b.
gold_text.609.4b: Some effects state that a player may do something “as though” some condition were true or a creature can do something “as though” some condition were true. This applies only to the stated effect. For purposes of that effect, treat the game exactly as if the stated condition were true. For all other purposes, treat the game normally. If an effect allows a player to spend mana “as though it were mana of any [type or color],” this affects only how the player may pay a cost. It doesn’t change that cost, and it doesn’t change what mana was actually spent to pay that cost. The same is true for effects that say “mana of any type can be spent.”
gold_text.702.137a: Spectacle Spectacle is a static ability that functions on the stack. “Spectacle [cost]” means “You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell’s mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn.” Casting a spell for its spectacle cost follows the rules for paying alternative costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h.

It doesn’t change that cost, and it doesn’t change what mana was actually spent to pay that cost. The same is true for effects that say “mana of any type can be spent.”

answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.
